text.0_Introduction, 0_Paragraph:
The author said:
It is a clear and well-known matter that belief in the knowledge of God, blessed be He, concerning the individual beings of the lower world and their particulars, and His providence over them both collectively and individually, are among the great foundations of the Torah of Moshe our teacher, peace be upon him.
text.0_Introduction, 1_Paragraph: For one who denies this and says that the Creator does not know the individual beings of the lower world and their particulars denies the Torah in its entirety. Likewise, one who denies Divine providence, saying that the Creator does not watch over human beings—whether they do good or evil, whether they experience benefit and salvation or suffering and disaster—and that all of this is merely accidental, not according to God’s will or intention toward them, also has no share in the World to Come and has no remembrance or merit in the Torah, neither in its commandments nor its warnings.
text.0_Introduction, 2_Paragraph: For if God does not take account of them, nor bring about the promised rewards and punishments, because He does not intend them, then there is also no basis for prophecy at all, since prophecy itself is a great form of Divine providence.
text.0_Introduction, 3_Paragraph: Rather, we must believe that God knows all individuals and all their details—the higher beings and the lower beings—their actions and their thoughts, those that have passed, those that exist now, and those that will happen in the future. For He is the One who creates them and brings them forth from absolute nothingness into the existence which they now possess.
text.0_Introduction, 4_Paragraph: We must firmly believe what Scripture says:
text.0_Introduction, 5_Paragraph: “For the Lord searches all hearts and understands every inclination of the thoughts.” (Divrei HaYamim I 28:9)
text.0_Introduction, 6_Paragraph: After this, we move to the belief in Divine providence and protection, and we affirm what Scripture says:
text.0_Introduction, 7_Paragraph: “Great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open upon all the ways of mankind, to give each person according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.” (Yirmiyahu 32:19)
text.0_Introduction, 8_Paragraph: Through this, our belief in Torah and mitzvot is established. For once we believe that God knows and supervises, our faith in prophecy follows. We believe that He, blessed be He, knows, supervises, commands, and warns—that is, He commands us to do what is good and upright and warns us against evil. He watches over us and fulfills for us all the good promises contained in the Torah, and brings upon those who transgress the punishments that He decrees upon them.
text.0_Introduction, 9_Paragraph: For this is truly fitting for the Creator’s relationship with His lower creatures: He did not create them for emptiness, nor did He fashion them merely by chance. Since they were created with purpose and will, it is appropriate that He should have desire and will concerning them and concerning their actions. His intention in creating them was not for nothing, but rather “for His glory He created them; He formed them and made them.”
text.0_Introduction, 10_Paragraph: Therefore, we believe in complete Divine providence, as in the verse:
text.0_Introduction, 11_Paragraph: “The eyes of the Lord roam throughout the entire earth, watching the wicked and the righteous.”
text.0_Introduction, 12_Paragraph: We also believe in miraculous providence—that is, the promises of the Torah and all miracles. For intellectually there is no difference between saying:
text.0_Introduction, 13_Paragraph: “So-and-so, a righteous person, will live out his days and live eighty years in tranquility,”
text.0_Introduction, 17_Paragraph: “Chananiah ben Azor was told: ‘This year you will die, because you have spoken rebellion against God.’”
text.0_Introduction, 18_Paragraph: This is no different, in principle, from the splitting of the Red Sea, the manna that fell for forty years, and all the miracles.
text.0_Introduction, 20_Paragraph:
“I will remove sickness from your midst,”
“I will send pestilence among you,”
“I will send wild beasts among you and they will destroy you,”
text.0_Introduction, 21_Paragraph: are equal in their nature to the plagues of the firstborn, the plague, the wild beasts, the drowning of Egypt in the sea, and:
text.0_Introduction, 22_Paragraph:
“For all the Children of Israel, no dog sharpened its tongue.”
“The Children of Israel walked on dry land within the sea.”
text.0_Introduction, 23_Paragraph: There is no difference between all of David son of Jesse’s prayers and our daily prayers, and all the miracles that occurred, except that some are hidden and some are public.
text.0_Introduction, 24_Paragraph: For if we say that nature itself sustains everything, then no person or animal ever dies because of merit or sin. But once we believe that God caused a person to die before his natural time, then the hand of God has performed a miracle and changed nature—just as He changed nature by splitting the sea before His people and drowning their enemies in it.
text.0_Introduction, 25_Paragraph: The difference between these is only that one is hidden and one is obvious.
text.0_Introduction, 26_Paragraph: And if we insist and say: “The person who ate terumah does not die through a supernatural change, but rather God arranged for him foods that produce illness, or he fell in war and died as normally happens,” then we are still admitting that his fortune was changed for the worse because of his sin, or for the better because of his merit—and nature is not the ultimate ruler.
text.0_Introduction, 27_Paragraph: And if God changes His decree because of a person’s sin, causing him to eat harmful foods that he would not have eaten had he not sinned, then it is even easier to say that He can change the nature of a normally good food and make it harmful to him.
text.0_Introduction, 29_Paragraph: “Only if the Lord strikes him, or his day comes and he dies, or he goes down into battle and perishes.” (I Samuel 26:10)
text.0_Introduction, 30_Paragraph: The plague is a change in nature caused by God striking him; war is also his death occurring through the decree of the Supreme One.
text.0_Introduction, 32_Paragraph:
“I will give your rains in their proper time,”
“God will open for you His good treasure,”
text.0_Introduction, 34_Paragraph:
“Your heavens above you shall be like copper,”
“God will give the rain of your land dust and powder,”
text.0_Introduction, 35_Paragraph: are all miracles that stand continually, changing the natural order and the power of the heavenly systems over the earth.
text.0_Introduction, 36_Paragraph: Likewise, the promises to the nation—for good or for punishment—are all established signs and wonders.
text.0_Introduction, 38_Paragraph: “They shall be signs and wonders upon you and upon your descendants forever.”
text.0_Introduction, 40_Paragraph: “All the nations of the earth shall see that the Name of the Lord is called upon you,”
text.0_Introduction, 41_Paragraph: because their goodness will exist through changes in nature unlike those experienced by all other nations.
